hlr.text: The application shall maintain a compile-time table of supported AVR Dx/Du/Sd device families (AVR-DA, AVR-DB, AVR-DD, AVR-DU, AVR-SD) where each entry records the family name, the base address and size of every programmable NVM window (EEPROM, USERROW, FUSES, LOCK), the SIGROW base address, and a boolean flag indicating whether the family has been hardware-validated on real silicon. On startup, after `updi_open()` and before any NVM operation, the application shall select an active device descriptor by one of two paths: (a) if the user supplied `--force-device=<family>` on the command line, the named entry shall be selected by case-insensitive match and a warning shall be emitted on `stderr` when the entry's `hw_tested` flag is false; (b) otherwise the application shall read the 3-byte SIGROW DEVICEID0..2 triplet at the AVR-DA/DB/DD canonical address (`0x1100`) and look it up against the table's autodetect signatures, failing with a diagnostic that names all five supported families and the `--force-device` option when DEVICEID0 is not `0x1E` or the signature is unrecognised. The AVR-DU and AVR-SD families place SIGROW at `0x1080` rather than `0x1100`, so they cannot be auto-detected from the AVR-DA probe address and shall always be selected via `--force-device`. Once selected, all subsequent NVM read/write call sites and the ELF-VMA window classifier in `load_segments()` shall consult the runtime-selected descriptor for window bases and sizes; no hard-coded address constant shall be used for the per-family fields. AVR-DA is the only family currently validated against live silicon; AVR-DB/DD/DU/SD entries are declared from the published datasheet memory maps and are marked untested-on-silicon. The diagnostic device mode (`--device`) shall tolerate unknown silicon — when no `--force-device` override is supplied it shall not invoke the autodetect probe so the report can still display raw SIGROW bytes for triage.

hlr.name: Lockbit Programming Safety Interlock
hlr.text: Writing the LOCK byte (UPDI window `0x820040`–`0x820043`) shall be subject to two mandatory safety interlocks. First, the application shall refuse to program the LOCK window unless `--erase` was also supplied on the command line, because the silicon requires a chip-erase to clear `LOCKSTATUS` before lockbits can be re-programmed and partial writes brick the part. Second, the application shall refuse any 4-byte LOCK payload other than the unlock pattern `0x5CC5C55C` (little-endian) unless the operator additionally supplies `--allow-lock-updi`, because every other 4-byte value risks setting the `UPDIDIS` lockbit which permanently disables the UPDI debug interface. When `LOCKSTATUS` (`ASI_SYS_STATUS` bit 1) is asserted at the time of the LOCK write, the application shall abort with the new error code `UPDI_ERR_LOCKED` (-3). With both interlocks satisfied (`--erase` present, payload is the unlock pattern OR `--allow-lock-updi` present), the application shall write the LOCK byte(s) using the same EEPROM `EEERWR` sequence as the other non-FLASH windows.

hlr.name: On-Target Hardware Integration Test Harness
hlr.text: The project shall provide a standalone, manual-only on-target hardware integration test harness, separate from the unit-test suite, that validates the UPDI driver, device-info report, SRAM and FLASH memory access, and the GDB RSP server against live AVR-Dx silicon. The harness shall be organised into four opt-in groups: Group A (read-only link and device-info probes), Group B (non-destructive SRAM round-trips with size and address-mode variants), Group C (destructive FLASH erase/write/verify, gated by an explicit confirmation variable), and Group D (RSP server spawn-and-probe over TCP, gated by an opt-in variable). The harness shall be configurable via environment variables and command-line flags (serial port, expected device ID, SRAM probe address, FLASH page address, RSP TCP port, verbosity), and shall accept an explicit `--addr-24bit` switch to validate 24-bit UPDI addressing on parts whose FLASH lies above 64 KiB. The Makefile shall expose dedicated targets `hw-test` (Groups A+B), `hw-test-nvm` (Groups A+B+C), `hw-test-rsp` (Groups A+B+D), and `hw-test-all` (all groups); none of these targets shall ever be invoked by `make test`.

hlr.name: Interactive Debug-Session Acceptance Suite
hlr.text: The on-target Group-G GDB acceptance harness (`tests/hw/gdb_acceptance.py`, driven by `make hw-test-gdb`) shall include a suite of cases that emulate a complete *interactive* debug session against live AVR-Dx silicon — exercising the combinations a developer drives by hand in an IDE (VS Code Cortex-Debug / `cppdbg`) rather than the isolated protocol primitives covered by the earlier Group-G cases. The suite shall run against a dedicated deterministic bare-metal fixture (`tests/fixtures/gdb_debug_session.c`) built at `-O0` with an explicit four-deep call chain `main -> top -> mid -> leaf`, `noinline` functions, scalar / struct / array globals plus a constant marker, and per-frame parameters and locals whose first-hit values are fixed constants; the fixture's known first-hit values are `leaf(7, 2)` returning `49397`, `leaf(7, 3)` returning `49405`, `g_marker = 49374`, `g_cfg = { base = 100, gain = -7 }`, and `g_arr = { 10, 20, 30, 40 }`. The suite shall verify: (a) a multi-frame backtrace that reaches `main` in correct frame order, plus frame selection (`frame N`, `up`, `down`) with per-frame `info args`; (b) source-level `step` (into a call), `next` (over a call), and `finish` (out of a frame) reporting the correct returned value; (c) multiple simultaneous breakpoints hit in call order (`top` then `mid` then `leaf`); (d) a conditional breakpoint (`break leaf if b == 3`) that skips the non-matching `leaf(7, 2)` call and stops only at `leaf(7, 3)`; (e) global reads of a scalar, a struct, and an array, including specific struct fields and array elements; (f) per-frame `info locals` and `info args` reading back the exact constants the fixture assigns; and (g) one capstone case that drives a realistic session start to finish. The fixture shall be flashed via the server's `--load` path and selected through a new `--dbg-elf` / `HW_GDB_DBG_ELF` knob; breakpoints shall be set by symbol (never by line number) so the suite is robust to edits in the fixture. The suite shall remain manual-only and shall never be wired into `make test`.

hlr.name: ELF and DWARF Parsing via elfutils
hlr.text: ELF and DWARF parsing shall be delegated to the **elfutils** libraries — libelf (accessed through the class-independent GElf API) for the ELF container and libdw for DWARF — rather than hand-decoded from raw byte layouts. `src/elf_parser.c` shall be a thin adapter that holds only the AVR-Dx/avrOS domain logic (avrOS system-table symbol discovery, the mapped-flash VMA→LMA translation, word-vs-byte flash addressing, and the Microchip deviceinfo note) on top of those libraries, so that ELF/DWARF format changes are absorbed by elfutils. The bundled ELF type shim (`src/elf.h`) is removed; ELF type definitions come from the system `<elf.h>` that elfutils provides. The module's public C API (`elf_open`, `elf_close`, `elf_find_avros_tables`, `elf_has_fsm_symbols`, `elf_flash_addr`, `elf_phys_flash_byte_addr`) and the `ElfContext` / `AvrOsSymbolIndex` contract consumed by `fsm_mapper` and `main` shall be preserved, with the libelf `Elf*` and libdw `Dwarf*` handles held as opaque `void*` so consumers need no elfutils headers.

hlr.name: DWARF Source-Level Lookup (DAP Groundwork)
hlr.text: The ELF module shall expose DWARF-backed source-level lookup so a future native Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP) front-end can map between machine addresses and source locations without delegating to `avr-gdb` (the GDB-RSP path does not use it). It shall provide: `elf_dwarf_available()` (returns 1, since elfutils is a required dependency); `elf_addr_to_line()` mapping a code byte address to its source file and 1-based line via libdw; and `elf_line_to_addr()` resolving a `file:line` (matched by basename) to the first code byte address. The accessors shall be safe to call when the ELF carries no debug info — returning -1 and leaving outputs untouched — and shall never abort the session. This requirement lands the source-mapping capability only; the DAP listener and request handlers are a later phase.

hlr.name: Protocol-Agnostic Debug Core
hlr.text: The server's debug logic shall be structured as a protocol-agnostic *debug core* — execution control, register and memory access, the hardware-comparator arbiter and software-breakpoint model, target (avrOS FSM) introspection, and ELF/DWARF — that is independent of any client-facing wire protocol. Client protocols shall be implemented as thin front-ends over this core: the existing GDB-RSP server (`src/gdb_rsp.c`) and, in future, a native DAP server intended to run in parallel. A front-end shall translate wire framing to and from the core's verbs and shall be the only layer that formats a protocol-specific reply; the core shall never emit RSP, DAP, or any other wire encoding, and shall never be reached *into* by a lower layer (per the SDD §2.2 layered-architecture rule, UPDI helpers never choose policy such as breakpoint slots). The core's protocol-neutral entry surface shall be reachable through a single aggregating include, `src/debug_core.h`. Phase 15 establishes this seam by aggregation; physically relocating the arbiter, stop-cause classifier, and software-breakpoint bodies out of the RSP module into a dedicated debug-core translation unit is deferred to the DAP-server phase to avoid destabilising the verified RSP path.

hlr.name: Front-End Protocol Selection (RSP/DAP)
hlr.text: The client-facing protocol front-end shall be selectable at startup via two mutually-exclusive command-line switches: `--rsp` (the GDB Remote Serial Protocol server, `src/gdb_rsp.c`) and `--dap` (the Debug Adapter Protocol server, `src/dap.c`). When neither switch is given the default shall be `--rsp`, preserving the historical behaviour of every existing invocation and test. Supplying both `--rsp` and `--dap` shall be rejected with a diagnostic and a non-zero exit. After argument parsing and target/ELF bring-up, the application shall dispatch to the selected front-end; both serve over the same TCP listener and the shared protocol-agnostic debug core (HLR-073). This requirement covers the selection and dispatch only; the DAP front-end's transport, lifecycle, and request handlers are specified by their own requirements as they are implemented (Phases 16–19).

hlr.name: DAP Wire Transport (Content-Length JSON-RPC)
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall exchange messages with the client using the Debug Adapter Protocol wire format: each message is a JSON object framed by a `Content-Length: <n>\r\n\r\n` header block followed by exactly `n` bytes of UTF-8 JSON body. On receive, the server shall consume the header block (matching the `Content-Length` field case-insensitively), then read exactly `n` body bytes — never over-reading into the following message — and shall reject a message whose advertised length is non-negative-overflowing or exceeds the receive buffer (`DAP_MSG_MAX`). On send, it shall prefix the body with the same header framing. JSON shall be handled by a self-contained recursive-descent tokenizer (no third-party JSON library is vendored — chosen so the parser is in-tree, in the project's C99 style, and directly unit-testable) exposing object-member lookup, string extraction with JSON-escape decoding, numeric extraction, and a string escaper for emission. The transport (framing + codec) shall be independent of the target and therefore unit-testable over a pipe/socketpair without hardware.

hlr.name: DAP Connection Lifecycle
hlr.text: The DAP front-end (`dap_serve()`, reached when the server is started with `--dap`) shall accept one client on the shared TCP listener and service it on the single `select()`-based event loop, honouring the global quit flag between messages. Over that connection it shall implement the DAP connection lifecycle: `initialize` (reply with the adapter capabilities — at minimum `supportsConfigurationDoneRequest` — then emit the `initialized` event); `launch` and `attach` (reply success; the target is already connected and in OCD debug mode, so attach/launch are equivalent here); `setBreakpoints` and `setExceptionBreakpoints` during the configuration phase (reply success — real breakpoint installation is Phase 18); `configurationDone` (halt the target and emit a `stopped` event with reason `entry` for thread 1, reaching the stopped-at-entry state); `threads` (report the single live CPU thread); and `disconnect`/`terminate` (resume the target and close the session). Every reply shall be a well-formed DAP `response` carrying the request's `seq` as `request_seq`, the `command`, and a `success` flag; a request the build does not yet implement shall receive a `success:false` response with a `message` (rather than silence), so the client is never left waiting. Each emitted message shall carry a monotonically increasing `seq`. UPDI side effects shall be skipped when no target link is present so the dispatch is unit-testable without hardware.

hlr.name: Debug-in-Sleep (preserve the wake source across the SW-breakpoint reset)
hlr.text: Installing or removing a software breakpoint requires a FLASH write, which on AVR-Dx must enter NVMPROG via a mandatory `ASI_RESET_REQ` system-reset pulse (the pulse latches the NVMProg key). That reset returns every peripheral to its default state — wiping whatever interrupt source the firmware had configured to wake itself from `SLEEP`. Consequently, after a SW-breakpoint flash patch on an already-initialised target, a firmware that idles in `SLEEP` (e.g. avrOS `sysSleep()` → `SLEEP_MODE_IDLE`) has no live wake source and never wakes, so the next breakpoint past the sleep is never reached. (Bench-confirmed: the LED state held before `SLEEP` stays frozen, and a raw `Z0`/`z0`/`Z0`/continue sequence reproduces it; hardware breakpoints — which do not touch FLASH — are unaffected.) To prevent this, the SW-breakpoint flash-patch sequence shall, by default, **snapshot the target peripheral I/O register window before the NVMPROG reset and write it back after re-entering OCD**, restoring the configured wake source regardless of which peripheral (timer, USART, pin-change, …) it is — the firmware need not even use a system tick. As a complementary measure the application shall also assert `CLK_REQ` (bit 0 of `ASI_SYS_CTRLA`) on entering OCD so the system clock keeps running through `SLEEP`. A `--sleep` command-line switch shall disable both behaviours, leaving native target sleep/power characteristics intact (for power-path debugging). This is a UPDI/OCD-layer behaviour and benefits both the GDB-RSP and DAP front-ends. (Sleep modes below IDLE — Standby/Power-Down — may additionally require `RUN_STBY`/`RUN_TIME` in the memory-mapped OCD control register; the exact AVR-Dx OCD-v1 location must be confirmed against `doc/reference/guesswork.md` and is out of scope here.)

hlr.name: DAP Execution Control, Stop Events & Shallow stackTrace
hlr.text: Over a connected DAP session (HLR-076), the DAP front-end shall expose run control and the run-state event stream, mapping each request to the debug-core execution verbs (the same OCD primitives the GDB-RSP front-end composes, HLR-073). It shall implement: `continue` — reply `{allThreadsContinued:true}`, emit a `continued` event, and resume the target (`updi_run()`); the server's idle event-loop tick shall then poll the OCD STOPPED status (`updi_ocd_poll_halted()`) and, on halt, emit a `stopped` event. `pause` — halt the target (`updi_halt()`) and emit `stopped` with reason `pause`. `stepIn` / `next` / `stepOut` — perform **source-line-granular** stepping (not a single OCD instruction) and emit `stopped` with reason `step`: `stepIn` advances to the next source line, descending into calls; `next` advances to the next source line in the current frame, stepping *over* calls (running to the return rather than into the callee, so stepping over a delay/loop is immediate); `stepOut` runs until the current function returns to its caller. These are built on the shared debug-core stepping primitives — `bp_step_range()` (single-step while the PC stays in a source line's address range, the same loop the GDB-RSP `vCont;r` uses) and the reserved stepping comparator (`RSP_HW_BP_STEP_SLOT`) to run to a return address without disturbing user breakpoints — with the line's address range from `elf_line_range()` and the return address from the CFI unwinder. `threads` — report the single live CPU thread (`{id:1,name:"cpu"}`); avrOS FSM tasks remain `monitor`-style introspection, surfaced in a later refinement. Every `stopped` event shall carry `threadId:1` and `allThreadsStopped:true`; the defined reasons are `entry` (configurationDone, HLR-076), `step`, `breakpoint` (a halt detected while the target was running), and `pause`. `terminate` shall additionally emit a `terminated` event before closing. The front-end shall also serve a **shallow `stackTrace`** — frame 0 only: the live PC read over OCD (`updi_ocd_read_pc()`), resolved to `file:line` via libdw (`elf_addr_to_line()`, HLR-072) and returned with a `source` object; when no target or no DWARF line is available it shall still return one frame so the client has a valid stack. `scopes` shall return an empty array (frame variables are Phase 19); deeper frames via DWARF CFI unwinding and real function names are Phase 18. All target side effects shall be guarded (`updi_fd >= 0`) so the dispatch is unit-testable over a socketpair without hardware.

hlr.name: DAP Source Breakpoints
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall implement `setBreakpoints` for source-level breakpoints, installed through the shared breakpoint core (debug_bp.h, HLR-054/055/016) — exactly the HW-comparator arbiter + SW-`BREAK` model the GDB-RSP front-end uses. For each requested `{line[,condition]}` against `arguments.source.path`, the adapter shall resolve the source line to a code byte address with libdw (`elf_line_to_addr()`, HLR-072) and, when a target is attached, install it via the core (`bp_insert`, `auto` mode: a free OCD comparator else a SW FLASH-`BREAK`). The response shall carry a `breakpoints` array — one entry per request in order, each with an `id`, a `verified` flag (true when resolved-and-installed), and the `line`. A `setBreakpoints` call shall **replace** the full breakpoint set for that source (the prior set for the same path is removed from silicon first). When the target later halts on an installed breakpoint, the `stopped` event (HLR-078) shall carry reason `breakpoint` and the matching `hitBreakpointIds`. On `disconnect`/`terminate` all installed breakpoints shall be removed from silicon before the target is resumed, so detach leaves it running free. The breakpoint table and install/remove shall be guarded by the target link so the dispatch is unit-testable without hardware. The adapter shall also implement `setInstructionBreakpoints` (advertising `supportsInstructionBreakpoints`): each entry's `instructionReference` (+ optional `offset`) is parsed to a code address and installed through the same core, replacing the prior instruction-breakpoint set; the response carries per-entry `{id,verified,instructionReference}`. Conditional breakpoints are HLR-081.

hlr.name: DAP Multi-Frame Stack Trace
hlr.text: The DAP front-end's `stackTrace` shall report the full call stack — not just the innermost frame — by unwinding through the target's DWARF Call-Frame-Information (`.debug_frame`). For the halted PC and each recovered caller it shall resolve `file:line` via libdw (HLR-072) and emit a DAP stack frame with a monotonic `id`, the enclosing function name (the `DW_TAG_subprogram` covering the PC, falling back to the raw address when none does), the PC as `instructionPointerReference`, and the source location. The unwind shall be driven by the per-PC Canonical-Frame-Address rule extracted from `.debug_frame` (CFA = value(reg) + offset, where reg is the AVR Y frame-pointer pair r28:r29 or SP=r32); libdw's high-level CFI executor (`dwarf_cfi_addrframe`) returns an error on AVR `.debug_frame`, so a minimal in-tree CFI interpreter shall provide the CFA rule. AVR's fixed stack conventions then recover each caller: the 2-byte word return address spans [CFA-1, CFA] (code byte PC = word << 1) and the caller's saved Y pair sits just below it (callee `push r28; push r29`). Unwinding shall stop at an invalid return address (out of the FLASH range, or where no CFI covers the PC — e.g. the C-runtime frame that called `main`), or at a bounded frame cap. With no target or no DWARF the handler shall still return the single innermost frame so the client has a valid stack.

hlr.name: DAP Conditional Breakpoints
hlr.text: A DAP source breakpoint (HLR-079) may carry a `condition` expression; the adapter shall evaluate it on the live target each time the breakpoint is hit and resume transparently when it is false, stopping only when it is true. The supported grammar is `<variable> <relop> <integer>` with `<relop>` one of `== != < <= > >=`. The variable shall be resolved to its data-space address, size, and signedness from DWARF at the halted PC — locals/parameters via their `DW_OP_breg28`(Y pair)/`DW_OP_fbreg`(CFA) location and globals via `DW_OP_addr` — read over OCD, and compared against the integer. When the condition is false the adapter shall step over the breakpoint and auto-resume (the target keeps running, no `stopped` event); when true, unevaluable (unknown variable, unsupported form, or a UPDI error), or for an unconditional breakpoint at the same PC, it shall stop and report the hit (a bad condition must never hide a breakpoint). Stepping over a breakpoint to resume shall reuse the shared single-step core (the GDB remove/single-step/insert sequence), so it is correct for HW-comparator and SW-`BREAK` breakpoints and for 16-/32-bit instructions alike.

hlr.name: DAP Scopes & Variables
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall implement `scopes` and `variables` for source-level state inspection. For a stopped target, `stackTrace` (HLR-080) records each frame's register context (CFA / Y pair / SP); `scopes` for a `frameId` shall return a **Locals** scope (the frame's parameters and locals, addresses resolved against that frame's registers), a **Registers** scope for the innermost frame (the live CPU r0–r31, SP, SREG, PC), and a **Globals** scope (the compilation unit's file-scope variables) — each carrying a `variablesReference`. `variables` shall expand a scope, or a structured reference, lazily: each variable is rendered to a value string by its DWARF type — scalars by encoding (signed/unsigned/char/bool/enum/float), pointers as hex, structs as `{field = v, …}`, arrays as `{v0, v1, …}` — and an aggregate (struct/union/array) carries a child `variablesReference` that expands to its members/elements. Values are read from the target over OCD (the mapped-flash data window routed through the flash mirror). variablesReference handles are invalidated whenever the target resumes (continue/step). All target access is guarded by the link so the dispatch is unit-testable without hardware.

hlr.name: DAP Evaluate (Watch / REPL)
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall implement `evaluate` for watch and REPL expressions over the loaded DWARF. An expression is a variable reference: an identifier (resolved in the given `frameId`'s scope, then file scope) followed by a chain of `.field` (struct/union member) and `[index]` (array element) accessors. The adapter shall resolve the expression to a data-space address and DWARF type, render its value (HLR-082), and reply with the `result`, a `variablesReference` (non-zero for an aggregate, so the client can drill in), and a `memoryReference`. An unresolvable or unreadable expression shall be answered `success:false` rather than a fabricated value.

hlr.name: DAP Memory & Set Variable
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall implement `readMemory`, `writeMemory`, and `setVariable`, advertising the corresponding capabilities. `readMemory` shall return base64 of `count` bytes from `memoryReference` + `offset` over the target data space (mapped-flash window via the flash mirror), marking unreadable bytes. `writeMemory` shall write base64 `data` to `memoryReference` + `offset` over the data space. `setVariable` shall write a scalar value (decimal or `0x`-hex) back to a named child of a Locals/Globals/aggregate reference, at the variable's resolved address and DWARF byte width, then re-render the stored value. Writes are confined to the writable data space and guarded by the target link.

hlr.name: VS Code Launch-Config Helper
hlr.text: To ease VS Code setup for the `--dap` front-end, `avrOSdb --emit-vscode-config` shall print a ready-to-use `launch.json` to stdout and exit, needing no target or ELF, so it can be redirected into a project's `.vscode/launch.json`. The primary configuration shall be a self-starting `request: "launch"` config (the `avrosdb` debug type with `program`/`serial`/`elf`/`port`) — the companion `avrosdb-dap` extension spawns `avrOSdb --dap` itself and attaches, so the user does not run the server separately — with a `request: "attach"` config (to a server on `127.0.0.1:<port>`) included as an alternative.

hlr.name: avrOS Introspection over DAP Custom Requests
hlr.text: The DAP front-end shall expose the target's avrOS runtime objects to a DAP client through three custom requests — DAP has no `monitor` console channel, so this is the DAP analogue of `monitor avros`: `avrosdb/fsmList` shall reply `{"fsms":[{"id","name","state","active"}]}`, `avrosdb/eventList` shall reply `{"events":[{"name","status"}]}` (a null status when the descriptor's status pointer is null), and `avrosdb/queueList` shall reply `{"queues":[{"id","capacity","elemSize"}]}`. The FSM list shall reuse the FSM-thread snapshot (`fsm_build_thread_list()` in `src/fsm_mapper.c`) — the same data the GDB-RSP front-end surfaces as virtual threads — so a slot with a null state-machine pointer is skipped rather than listed. The event and queue lists shall decode the avrOS `EVNT_TABLE` / `QUE_TABLE` FLASH descriptor tables. To implement that decode in one place and keep the DAP front-end from depending on the GDB-RSP one, the event/queue table reader shall live in a protocol-agnostic introspection core (`src/avros.c`) that depends only on the UPDI and ELF layers; both these DAP custom requests and the GDB-RSP `monitor avros events|queues` formatter shall call it, per the SDD §2.2 layered-architecture rule (downward-only calls, no front-end → front-end dependency). Each request shall degrade gracefully — with no target link or no avrOS symbol tables it shall return an empty array rather than an error — and all target access shall be guarded by `updi_fd >= 0` so the dispatch is unit-testable without hardware. A null event-name pointer shall render the name as `<null>`, preserving the existing monitor output. The `--no-introspect` switch shall disable these custom requests on the DAP front-end exactly as it disables avrOS introspection on the GDB-RSP front-end: when introspection is disabled the server passes a NULL symbol index (and NULL FSM context) to `dap_serve()`, so all three requests return empty arrays.

section.title: CI-Grade Loader and Link Diagnostics
section.intro: Requirements in this section govern the Phase 9 features that turn the loader into a CI-trustable build/flash step and elevate the `--device` mode into a first-line link-health probe. They were tracked as GitHub issue #28 and implement the design narrative from the Phase 9 overview paragraph in the SDD.

hlr.name: Read-Back Verify After Load
hlr.text: After every successful `--load` write, the application shall re-read each programmed NVM range through the existing UPDI read path and compare the read-back bytes against the ELF payload. Verify shall cover the FLASH, EEPROM, USERROW, and FUSES windows; segments classified as SIGROW (read-only) or LOCK (read-once / write-only-after-erase) shall be skipped. On mismatch the application shall print one diagnostic line per failing page to `stderr` carrying the window name, page-aligned VMA, expected and actual IEEE 802.3 CRC32 values; shall not call `updi_enter_debug()`; shall not call `rsp_listen()`; and shall exit with status `UPDI_EXIT_VERIFY_FAIL` (`2`, distinct from the existing exit code `1` reserved for I/O / configuration failures). Verify shall be enabled by default for `--load` and `--prog`; the operator may disable it with the new `--no-verify` flag, in which case the application shall behave exactly as before Phase 9.

hlr.name: Program-and-Exit Mode
hlr.text: The application shall provide a new operating mode, activated by the `--prog` command-line flag and mutually exclusive with both `--device` and `--load`, that programs the supplied ELF into NVM, verifies the write per HLR-049, and exits — no GDB TCP listener shall be bound, no `updi_enter_debug()` shall be issued, and the target shall be left running with the UPDI link closed cleanly. On start-up the mode shall emit a single `baud=<N>` line on `stdout` reporting the negotiated UART rate. During programming the mode shall render an in-place single-line progress indicator (`[####....] %% page N/M phase window`) when `stdout` is a TTY (detected by `isatty(STDOUT_FILENO)`), and shall degrade to one line per page (or per phase transition) when `stdout` is piped or redirected. On verify success the mode shall print `verify: OK` and exit with status 0; on verify failure it shall exit with status `UPDI_EXIT_VERIFY_FAIL` (`2`); on any I/O or NVM failure it shall exit with status 1. Intended use is `avrOSdb --prog <serial-device> <elf-file>` from a CI script or a Makefile `flash:` target.

hlr.name: Fuses Pretty-Printer in Device Mode
hlr.text: The `--device` diagnostic mode shall, after printing the SIGROW / REVID / ASI status report defined by HLR-044, read the target's full FUSES window and the 4-byte LOCK window through the UPDI NVM read path and emit a human-readable decode to `stdout`. The decode shall consist of a header line (`Fuses (<family>, <N> bytes):`), one indented line per known fuse byte showing the offset, fuse name, and raw hex value, followed by indented sub-lines naming each documented bit-field (e.g. `WDTCFG.PERIOD = 8K`, `BODCFG.SLEEP = SAMPLED`, `OSCCFG.CLKSEL = OSCHF`, `SYSCFG0.CRCSRC`, `SYSCFG1.SUT`, `CODESIZE`, `BOOTSIZE`) using human-readable enum names rather than raw hex. Fuse bytes for which no bit-field decoder is registered shall be shown as `(reserved) raw=0x..`. The lock byte shall be shown on a final line `Lock: 0xXXXXXXXX (UNLOCKED|LOCKED)`, where `UNLOCKED` is the 4-byte little-endian value `0x5CC5C55C` and any other value is reported as `LOCKED`. The decode tables shall live alongside `g_device_table[]` in `src/updi.c` so they are selected by the same `updi_select_device()` runtime path. Phase 9 ships the AVR-DA / AVR-DB family table; other families fall back to raw hex with no per-bit decoding.

hlr.name: Auto-Baud Link-Quality Probe in Device Mode
hlr.text: The `--device` diagnostic mode shall, before opening the UPDI session, walk a fixed baud-rate ladder (`230400, 200000, 150000, 115200, 57600, 38400, 19200`) and at each rung open the UART at the candidate rate, issue a small fixed UPDI transaction sequence (`LDCS ASI_STATUSA`, repeated for a small sample window — default 8 samples), and record the byte error rate. Each rung result shall be reported to `stdout` as one line ` baud=<N> errors=<K>/<total>`. The application shall select the highest-rate rung that observed zero errors over the sample window; if no rung observes zero errors the probe shall report failure and the application shall fall back to the user-supplied or default baud rate. The probe shall be read-only — no NVM, no fuses, no system-reset paths, no `updi_enter_debug()` — and shall close every interim UART file descriptor it opens. The operator may disable the probe with the new `--no-autobaud` flag, in which case `--device` shall behave exactly as before Phase 9 and use `cfg.baud_rate` directly. The probe is invoked from `--device` mode only; `--load` and `--prog` continue to use the explicit `--baud` setting.

section.title: GDB Protocol Completion (avarice Feature Parity)
section.intro: Requirements in this section govern the Phase 10 features that bring `avrOSdb`'s GDB Remote Serial Protocol surface up to functional parity with the legacy `avarice` JTAG/dW stub: equivalent monitor verbs, equivalent `(gdb) load`, equivalent watchpoint and software-breakpoint experience, and equivalent extended-remote lifecycle. Wire-level drop-in compatibility with `avarice`-specific scripts is an explicit non-goal. Tracked as GitHub issue #31; implements the design narrative from the Phase 10 overview paragraph in the SDD.

hlr.name: Flash Programming via GDB load
hlr.text: The application shall implement the GDB `vFlashErase:addr,length`, `vFlashWrite:addr:XX...`, and `vFlashDone` packets so that the standard `(gdb) load` command programs the AVR FLASH directly from the running GDB session without exiting to an external programmer. On `vFlashErase` the server shall reject any address range that falls outside the FLASH window of the runtime-selected device (HLR-048) with reply `E22`; ranges that fall in EEPROM, USERROW, FUSES, LOCK, or SIGROW shall be refused for the same reason because `gdb load` carries no per-window verb to disambiguate. Erase shall be performed page-aligned via `updi_nvm_erase_flash_page()`; `vFlashWrite` shall accumulate the binary payload into the corresponding page buffer and program it with `updi_nvm_write_flash()`; `vFlashDone` shall flush any pending page, call `updi_enter_debug()` to leave the CPU halted at reset, and reply `OK`. The session's hardware-breakpoint shadow (`RspContext.hw_bp_addr[]`) and SW-breakpoint shadow (HLR-054) shall be cleared on `vFlashDone` because their underlying instructions may have been overwritten by the load. While a `vFlash*` transaction is in progress the server shall not service `g`/`G`/`m`/`M`/`c`/`s` packets; if such a packet arrives between `vFlashErase` and `vFlashDone` the server shall reply `E22` and discard the in-progress page buffers.

hlr.name: True Software Breakpoints via Flash BREAK Opcode
hlr.text: The application shall support an unbounded number of simultaneous software breakpoints by patching the AVR `BREAK` opcode (`0x9598`, little-endian) into the FLASH word at the target address on `Z0` and restoring the original 2-byte instruction on `z0`. A per-session shadow map shall record `(gdb_addr, flash_byte_addr, original_opcode_lo, original_opcode_hi, page_aligned_base)` for every active SW breakpoint so removal is exact. The patch sequence shall preserve live CPU state across the unavoidable OCD → NVMPROG → OCD transition: before NVMPROG entry the server shall snapshot R0–R31, SREG, SP, and PC via the OCD register file; after re-entering OCD it shall restore them with the existing `updi_ocd_write_*` primitives. SW breakpoints in the SIGROW, FUSES, USERROW, EEPROM, or LOCK windows shall be refused with `E22` because the AVR `BREAK` opcode is only meaningful when fetched as an instruction. The default breakpoint policy is `auto` (HLR-055): a `Z0` in FLASH shall be installed on a free OCD HW comparator (HLR-016) when one is available — avoiding the FLASH write, and therefore the NVMPROG system-reset glitch and the peripheral save/restore of HLR-077, entirely, and keeping the breakpoint valid while the target sleeps — and shall fall back to the FLASH-`BREAK` patch only once the single user comparator is occupied. The operator may force the FLASH-patch path for every `Z0` with `monitor avros bp-mode sw`, or opt out of true SW breakpoints altogether with `monitor avros bp-mode hw-only` (HLR-055), in which case `Z0` shall continue to alias to the two HW comparators (the Phase 1–8 behaviour mandated by HLR-016); the mode shall persist across detach/reattach for the lifetime of the server process. On `vFlashDone` (HLR-053) and on `monitor reset` / `monitor chip-erase` (HLR-055) every SW breakpoint shadow entry shall be discarded because the underlying instruction is no longer present in FLASH.

hlr.name: avarice-Compatible Monitor Commands
hlr.text: The application shall expose a top-level set of `monitor` verbs that mirror the `avarice` command surface, so that GDB scripts written for `avarice` work unchanged: `monitor reset` (issue `updi_reset()` and leave the CPU halted at the reset vector, then invalidate the FSM snapshot cache so the next introspection read reflects post-reset state), `monitor halt` (call `updi_halt()` and reply with the same `T05thread:<id>;` packet as a step boundary), `monitor go` (call `updi_run()` and reply `OK` — the subsequent stop-reason packet is emitted when the CPU next halts), `monitor erase` and `monitor chip-erase` (issue `updi_chip_erase()`, but only when the server was launched with the new `--allow-erase` flag — without that flag the verb shall reply with an O-packet diagnostic and `E22`), `monitor version` (one O-packet line carrying the server version, git short SHA, build date, and the active device family name from HLR-048), `monitor bp-mode <auto|sw|hw-only>` (configure the breakpoint installation policy per HLR-054 — `auto`, the default, prefers a free HW comparator and falls back to the SW FLASH-`BREAK` patch; `sw` forces the FLASH patch; `hw-only` aliases `Z0` to the HW comparators), and `monitor help` (one O-packet per recognised verb summarising syntax and side-effects, terminating with `OK`). The dispatcher in `src/monitor.c` shall continue to route the `avros ` prefix to the existing avrOS-specific handlers (`events`, `queues`); unknown verbs shall reply with the existing usage hint plus `E22`. None of the new verbs shall alter the FSM snapshot path other than via the explicit cache invalidation noted above.

hlr.name: Hardware Data Watchpoints
hlr.text: The application shall reply with the empty RSP packet (`$#00`) to the GDB watchpoint requests `Z2`/`z2` (write), `Z3`/`z3` (read), and `Z4`/`z4` (access). The empty reply is the documented RSP signal for "feature unsupported" and causes GDB to fall back transparently to software watchpoints (single-step + memory poll), so the user-visible `watch <expr>` command continues to work. The empty-packet behaviour reflects a silicon constraint: the AVR-Dx OCD exposed over UPDI provides only the program-counter breakpoint comparators (`OCD_BP0A` / `OCD_BP1A`) and does NOT expose any data-address comparator hardware. The conclusion is confirmed by four independent sources: (1) the FF-bomb experiment in `doc/reference/guesswork.md`, which finds writable bits only at `BP0A`, `BP1A`, `CTRL0`, `CTRL1`, `STATUS0/1`, `INSN0/1`, `PC`, `SP`, `SREG`, and the register file; (2) the canonical open-source AVR debugger Bloom, whose UPDI driver declares `hardwareBreakpoints=1` and exposes no `setDataWatchpoint` method; (3) the sibling SerialUPDI debugger `feline-felicity/avr-absurd`, whose feature list documents "Two hardware breakpoints" and no watchpoints; and (4) Microchip's own `mraardvark/pyavrdebug` (CMSIS-DAP / Atmel-ICE stack), whose Z-packet handler explicitly replies the empty packet for Z2/Z3/Z4 — i.e. even the proprietary EDBG protocol over a debugger pod does not expose data watchpoints. The server shall not advertise any watchpoint-related capability in its `qSupported` reply.

hlr.name: Extended-Remote Lifecycle Packets
hlr.text: The application shall support the `target extended-remote` connection mode by implementing the `vRun;<arg>;<arg>...` packet (treat the first argument as a path to a new `.elf` file, swap it into the existing `AppConfig`, re-run ELF parsing, re-build the FSM context, and reply with a `T05` stop at the new reset vector), the `vAttach;<pid>` packet (reply `OK` followed by the standard stop-reply; `pid` is informational only on a single-target stub), and the `vKill;<pid>` packet (call `updi_run()` to release the target, close the GDB client fd, and return to the listen state without exiting the server process). Existing `D` (detach) and `k` (kill) handlers shall remain operational; `k` shall continue to mean process-exit so that scripts that hard-stop the server keep working. The `qSupported` feature string shall be extended with `vRun+;vAttach+;vKill+`. The server shall **not** advertise `multiprocess+`: it presents a single GDB thread (the live CPU), so multiprocess thread-id forms are unnecessary, and avrOS FSM state is exposed via introspection (`monitor avros tasks`, HLR-029 et seq.) rather than as GDB threads.

hlr.name: Protocol Cleanup — qC, qOffsets, T, R
hlr.text: The application shall stop replying with the empty packet for the standard small queries that `avarice` answers but Phase 1–8 leaves unimplemented, because some IDE configurations promote the resulting `unsupported feature` warnings to fatal errors. Specifically: `qC` shall return `QC<tid>` where `<tid>` is the currently selected `c`-thread (or `0` when no thread is selected); `qOffsets` shall return `Text=0;Data=0;Bss=0` because the AVR reset vector is fixed at address zero and no position-independent loading is performed; `T<tid>` (is-thread-alive) shall return `OK` for the single live-CPU thread (TID 1) and `E01` otherwise; and `R<XX>` (RCmd restart) shall behave as `monitor reset` followed by `c` and reply with the resulting stop packet. None of these handlers shall alter execution state beyond the explicit semantics above.

hlr.name: vKill Listener Survival
hlr.text: The `vKill[;<pid>]` packet shall close the GDB client connection but shall not terminate the avrOSdb server process. After replying `OK` and closing the client `fd`, `event_loop()` shall return to its `select()` loop and continue listening on the configured TCP port for a new GDB session. This makes avrOSdb honest about the GDB extended-remote contract: `vKill` ends the *debug session*, not the *debugger*, so a subsequent F5 / `target extended-remote :1234` from the same operator shall succeed without restarting the server. Concretely, `dh_vkill()` shall: (a) call `updi_halt()` on the target so the next session attaches to a stopped CPU; (b) release both AVR-Dx OCD hardware-breakpoint comparators via `rsp_hw_bp_clear_all()`; (c) drop the per-session software-breakpoint shadow via `rsp_sw_bp_clear_all()` (FLASH BREAK rewrite is not required — the shadow is purely host-side bookkeeping per LLR-RSP-30 et seq.); (d) reply `OK`; (e) record `ctx->disconnect_reason = "vKill"` for the lifecycle logger (HLR-065); (f) close the GDB socket via `*ctx->gdb_fd_p` and set the pointed-at fd to `-1`. The handler shall **not** set `*ctx->quit_p = 1`. The `--prog` mode (HLR-019/Phase 8) is unaffected: it never opens the GDB listener and never reaches `dh_vkill()`. The pre-Phase-11 legacy `k` packet path (`dh_detach` with `pkt[0] == 'k'`) is preserved and still sets `quit_p = 1` so existing operators relying on `kill` to shut the server down retain that behaviour.

hlr.name: swbreak/hwbreak Stop-Cause Tags
hlr.text: The application shall classify every halt and tag the resulting `T05` stop reply with the GDB Remote Serial Protocol stop-cause field that names the cause, so that `avr-gdb` (and front-ends layered on it, in particular VS Code `cppdbg`) can distinguish a software breakpoint hit from a hardware comparator hit from a single-step completion from a host-issued interrupt without a target-side guess. Concretely: (a) the `qSupported` reply shall advertise `swbreak+;hwbreak+` in addition to the existing capability set; (b) a new `enum RspStopCause` shall enumerate `SC_NONE`, `SC_SWBREAK`, `SC_HWBREAK`, `SC_STEP`, `SC_INTR`; (c) every default handler that emits a `T<sig>thread:<tid>;` stop reply (`dh_halt_reason`, the post-`vCont;c`/`c` halt path inside `dh_continue`, `dh_step`, and the indirect emitters `dh_vrun` and `dh_vattach` which delegate to `dh_halt_reason`) shall route through a single formatter that, after the `T<sig>` and before the `thread:` field, inserts `swbreak:;` when the cause is `SC_SWBREAK` and `hwbreak:;` when the cause is `SC_HWBREAK`; `SC_STEP`, `SC_INTR`, and `SC_NONE` shall produce no extra tag (the existing bare `T05`/`T02` semantics). Classification rules: read the live PC via `updi_ocd_read_pc()` after the halt has settled; if the PC matches any in-use `RspContext.sw_bp[i].addr` slot the cause is `SC_SWBREAK`; otherwise if the PC matches either `RspContext.hw_bp_addr[i]` slot the cause is `SC_HWBREAK`; otherwise the cause is `SC_INTR` when the local `got_ctrl_c` flag is set inside `dh_continue` (or when `OCD_STATUS1_EXTBRK` is set as observed by `signal_for_halt_status()`), `SC_STEP` when the halt arrived via `dh_step()`, and `SC_NONE` for the bare `?` probe. The classifier shall not adjust PC — GDB performs the BREAK-instruction PC rewind itself when it sees `swbreak:;`. The classifier shall preserve the layered architecture (SDD §2.2): it lives entirely in `src/gdb_rsp.c` and reads silicon only via the existing `updi_ocd_*` helpers. Backward compatibility: the tag is informational; older `avr-gdb` releases that do not advertise `swbreak+`/`hwbreak+` in their own `qSupported` ignore the extra field per the GDB RSP spec, so emission can remain unconditional.

hlr.name: Lifecycle Logging
vCont;r Range Step
hlr.text: The `vCont` packet handler shall accept the `r<start>,<end>[:<thread>]` action and implement GDB's range-step semantics: keep single-stepping the target one instruction at a time so long as the live PC remains inside the half-open range `[start, end)`. When the PC leaves that range — or the user issues a Ctrl-C interrupt — the handler shall halt and emit a single stop reply identical in form to the `vCont;s` reply (a `T05`/`T02` packet with the `swbreak`/`hwbreak`/`step`/`intr` cause classification per HLR-062). `start` and `end` are GDB code addresses (Flash, no `0x800000` data flag); both are 32-bit hex without the `0x` prefix in the wire packet. The `vCont?` probe reply shall be extended from `vCont;c;s` to `vCont;c;s;r` so GDB's range-step optimisation activates. The handler shall reuse the existing OCD STATUS poll cadence (5 ms) for Ctrl-C detection; per-step PC reads use `updi_ocd_read_pc()`. As a safety net, an unbounded loop shall be capped at `RSP_RANGE_STEP_MAX = 100000` iterations to defend against a runaway target whose PC never exits the range; reaching the cap shall halt the target and emit a normal `T05` reply (the user will see no progress and can investigate). Range-step does not require breakpoint installation: it is a software loop driven entirely by the host. Backward compatibility: GDB clients that do not negotiate `vCont;r` continue to receive the prior `vCont;c;s` advertisement-equivalent behaviour because they never send `vCont;r` in the first place.

hlr.name: qXfer:memory-map:read+ Advertisement
hlr.text: The RSP server shall advertise `qXfer:memory-map:read+` in its `qSupported` reply and shall service `qXfer:memory-map:read::<offset>,<length>` requests by returning a GDB memory-map XML document describing the seven AVR-Dx memory regions visible to GDB: Flash, SRAM, EEPROM, FUSES, LOCK, SIGROW, and USERROW. The Flash region shall be expressed with `start="0x0"`, `length=<flash_size>`, and a `<property name="blocksize">` child set to the AVR-Dx Flash page size (`UPDI_FLASH_PAGE_SIZE` = 512 bytes). The SRAM region shall be expressed with `type="ram"`, `start=<sram_base>`, and `length=<sram_size>`, where `sram_base` is the GDB-side data-space address (already carrying the AVR `0x00800000` data-space flag, sourced verbatim from the second `PT_LOAD` segment of the supplied ELF). Flash and SRAM sizes shall be sourced from `RspContext.flash_size` / `.sram_base` / `.sram_size`, which `main.c` populates from the parsed ELF at session init. The five non-FLASH NVM regions are AVR-Dx device-class constants and shall be advertised at their GDB-visible ELF VMA bands (the same bands `load_segments()` in `src/main.c` already recognises for M-packet routing): EEPROM at `ELF_VMA_EEPROM = 0x810000` length `UPDI_EEPROM_SIZE = 0x200`, FUSES at `ELF_VMA_FUSES = 0x820000` length `UPDI_FUSES_SIZE = 0x10`, LOCK at `ELF_VMA_LOCK = 0x830000` length `UPDI_LOCK_SIZE = 0x4`, SIGROW at `ELF_VMA_SIGROW = 0x840000` length `UPDI_SIGROW_SIZE = 0x40`, USERROW at `ELF_VMA_USERROW = 0x850000` length `UPDI_USERROW_SIZE = 0x20`. EEPROM, FUSES, and LOCK shall be typed `flash` with `blocksize=0x1` (byte-granular host-side erase/write window — the silicon-side page programming is hidden by `updi.c`); USERROW shall be typed `flash` with `blocksize=UPDI_USERROW_SIZE` (whole-row write semantics on AVR-Dx); SIGROW shall be typed `rom` (read-only, no blocksize). The non-FLASH regions appear whenever the Flash or SRAM region is present. Additionally, when an avrOS ELF symbol index is available (so the server can translate it — see HLR-067), the map shall advertise the AVR-Dx mapped-flash data window — the high half of the 16-bit data space (data >= 0x8000) into which FLASH is aliased and where avr-gcc places `.rodata` — as a read-only `rom` region at GDB address `0x808000` (the `0x00800000` data-space flag OR'd with the `0x8000` window base) with length `min(flash_size, 0x8000)`. Advertising this window is required so GDB will *issue* reads of flash-resident string literals (e.g. an avrOS FSM `currStateName`) rather than refusing them client-side as undescribed memory. When the server is started without an ELF (or the ELF lacks both a Flash and a SRAM `PT_LOAD`), the handler shall reply `l` (end-of-transfer with no payload) and GDB shall fall back to its built-in defaults rather than receive a fabricated map. The reply shall honour the standard `qXfer` framing: a leading `m` for "more data follows" or `l` for "last chunk", followed by the raw XML bytes from `[offset, offset+length)` of the rendered document. Malformed `<offset>,<length>` syntax (missing comma, non-hex digits) shall produce `E00`. The XML shall be re-rendered per request into a stack buffer (no heap, no caching) so the handler is reentrant and stateless.

hlr.name: Memory-Map Honesty for `m`-Reads
hlr.text: The RSP server's `m<addr>,<len>` read handler shall enforce that every read request lies entirely within one of the memory regions it advertised via `qXfer:memory-map:read+` (HLR-063), and shall reply with the GDB error code `E14` (the conventional `EFAULT` mapping for "memory inaccessible") whenever any byte of the requested range falls outside every advertised region. This honesty contract exists because GDB's stack-unwind logic — used by `finish`, `step-out`, and frame-walking — reads the saved return address off the target's stack via DWARF CFI and then plants a temporary breakpoint at the address it reads; if the server fabricates filler bytes (e.g. `0xff`) for an out-of-range address, GDB will install a temp breakpoint at a fabricated location and hang waiting for it to fire. The check shall be performed against the same `RspContext.flash_size` / `.sram_base` / `.sram_size` fields HLR-063 uses to build its advertisement and shall include all seven advertised regions (Flash, SRAM, EEPROM, FUSES, LOCK, SIGROW, USERROW) using the AVR-Dx device-class constants and ELF VMA bands defined in HLR-063. Backward-compatibility: when both `flash_size` and `sram_size` are zero — the same condition under which HLR-063 publishes no map and GDB falls back to its built-in defaults — the bounds check shall be bypassed and the historical permissive behaviour of `m` shall be preserved (so the no-ELF startup mode and `tests/hw/gdb_acceptance.py` continue to work). Mapped-flash exception: a data-space read in the AVR-Dx mapped-flash window (the GDB data-space flag set and the 16-bit offset >= 0x8000, the window HLR-063 advertises as `rom`) targets FLASH aliased into the data space — the case that left an avrOS `stateMachine->currStateName` unreadable. Such a read shall be served from the physical flash LMA by translating the 16-bit mapped VMA through the ELF index's `flash_lma_off` and routing it via the UPDI flash mirror (`flash_to_updi`), the same translation `fsm_mapper` uses for state-name strings; because that window is read-only FLASH and always present, the read shall be handled before — and shall bypass — the advertised-region SRAM-fault check above. This translation is available only when the ELF symbol index is present; without it the read falls through to the ordinary data-space path. Validation: the check shall be implemented in `dh_read_mem` only; symmetric enforcement on `M` / `X` writes is deliberately deferred to a future requirement because writes do not feed GDB's stack-unwind path. The arithmetic shall reject `len == 0` and shall detect 32-bit address-plus-length wrap-around so a malicious or malformed packet cannot bypass the check by overflow.

function.title: Introduction
function.name: intro
function.intro: Each LLR ID follows the pattern `LLR-XXX-NN`, where `XXX` is a module code and `NN` is a zero-padded two-digit sequence number. Module codes: `MAIN` (`src/main.c`), `UPDI` (`src/updi.c`), `RSP` (`src/gdb_rsp.c`), `ELF` (`src/elf_parser.c`), `FSM` (`src/fsm_mapper.c`), `MON` (`src/monitor.c`), `INST` (`Makefile`, `doc/avrOSdb.1`, `doc/UserManual.md`), `HWTEST` (`tests/hw/hw_test.c`). IDs are permanent contracts and may not be renumbered or reused once allocated.

function.title: src/main.c — Entry Point and Event Loop
function.name: main
function.intro: Requirements for `main()`, `parse_args()`, and `event_loop()`. These functions own the application lifecycle from argument parsing through resource cleanup.

llr.text: `parse_args()` shall populate an `AppConfig` struct from `argc`/`argv`. If any unrecognised argument is encountered, it shall print a usage message to `stderr` and call `exit(1)`.

When not supplied on the command line, `parse_args()` shall apply the following defaults to the `AppConfig` fields: `gdb_port` = 1234, `baud_rate` = 115200, `load_flash` = false. The `<serial-device>` and `<elf-file>` positional arguments are mandatory; absence of either shall trigger the usage error path.

`main()` shall call `updi_open()` and validate the returned file descriptor before calling `rsp_listen()`. A failure from either shall cause `main()` to release any already-open resources and return exit code 1.

When the `--load` flag is set, `main()` shall iterate over all `PT_LOAD` ELF program headers and call `updi_nvm_write_flash()` for each segment whose `p_filesz > 0` and whose virtual address lies below the SRAM base (i.e. flash-resident segments only). Segments with `p_vaddr >= ctx.sram_base` shall be skipped. All qualifying segments shall be written before entering `event_loop()`. A flash write failure shall cause `main()` to print an error to `stderr` and return exit code 1.

`event_loop()` shall multiplex `listen_fd`, `gdb_fd`, and `updi_fd` using a single POSIX `select()` call with no timeout. On each iteration it shall: accept a GDB client on `listen_fd` if `gdb_fd` is -1; forward console bytes from `updi_fd` to `stdout` via `updi_console_poll()`; dispatch RSP packets from `gdb_fd` via `rsp_recv_packet()` and `rsp_dispatch()`. No POSIX threads shall be created.

`main()` shall register a `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM` handler that sets the global `volatile sig_atomic_t g_quit` flag to 1. `event_loop()` shall test `g_quit` at the top of each loop iteration and return immediately when the flag is set, without closing any file descriptors itself.

On all exit paths, `main()` shall release resources in this exact order: (1) `rsp_close(cfg.gdb_fd)` if `gdb_fd >= 0`, (2) `rsp_close(cfg.listen_fd)`, (3) `elf_close(&ctx)`, (4) `updi_close(cfg.updi_fd)`. The process shall exit with code 0 on normal termination and code 1 on any fatal initialisation or flash-write failure.

`parse_args()` shall recognise the `--device` long option, set `cfg->device_info = true`, and accept the absence of the `<elf-file>` operand without error. Specifying both `--device` and `--load` on the same command line shall cause `parse_args()` to print `"error: --device is mutually exclusive with --load"` to `stderr`, print the usage synopsis, and call `exit(1)`.

When `cfg.device_info` is true, `main()` shall: (1) call `updi_open()`; (2) on success call `updi_read_device_info()`; (3) on success format and print to `stdout` a multi-line report containing `Serial device:`, `Baud rate:`, `Signature:` (3 hex bytes), `Family:` (looked up via a static `device_family[]` table indexed by signature \u2014 unknown signatures shall print `unknown device`), `Revision:`, `Serial:` (10 hex bytes), and `UPDI status: SYS_STATUS=0x.. KEY_STATUS=0x.. STATUSB=0x..`; (4) call `updi_close()` and return. The function shall **not** call `rsp_listen()`, `elf_find_avros_tables()`, `fsm_build_thread_list()`, or `event_loop()`. On any UPDI failure the function shall print a verbose diagnostic to `stderr` that names the failed step (e.g. `"updi-open"`, `"sigrow"`, `"sys-status"`) and return exit code 1.

Before entering `event_loop()`, `main()` shall call `updi_enter_debug(cfg.updi_fd)`, after `updi_open()` and any optional `updi_nvm_write_flash()` (`--load`) steps and before `rsp_listen()`. A non-zero return shall be treated as a fatal initialisation failure and shall trigger the LLR-MAIN-07 teardown with exit code 1. This arms AVR-Dx OCD mode for the lifetime of the server so that all RSP `g`/`G`/`P`/`s`/`c`/`Z0`/`Z1` operations have a halted, OCD-addressable CPU register file available on first use.

When `cfg.load_flash` is true, `load_segments()` shall walk every `PT_LOAD` segment of the open ELF context and classify it by its UPDI virtual address (after folding ELF VMAs below `UPDI_FLASH_BASE` into the FLASH window via `vaddr | 0x800000`). SRAM-resident segments shall be skipped silently. The classifier shall obtain its EEPROM, USERROW, FUSES, LOCK, and SIGROW window bases and sizes from the runtime-selected device descriptor (`updi_get_device()`, see LLR-UPDI-27); no per-family address shall be hard-coded in the classifier. SIGROW segments shall be skipped with a `"SIGROW segment @0x%06x ignored (read-only)"` notice on `stdout`. FLASH segments (everything below the selected device's USERROW base in the UPDI space) shall be padded with `0xFF` to a 512-byte page boundary and dispatched to `updi_nvm_write_flash()` — the established Phase 2/3 path is unchanged. EEPROM, USERROW, and FUSES segments shall be dispatched verbatim (no padding) to `updi_nvm_write_eeprom()`, `updi_nvm_write_userrow()`, and `updi_nvm_write_fuses()` respectively. LOCK segments (`[dev->lock_base, dev->lock_base + dev->lock_size)`) shall additionally require `cfg.erase_chip` to be true (else the function shall return -1 with a diagnostic naming the missing `--erase` flag) and shall be dispatched to `updi_nvm_write_lockbits(..., cfg.allow_lock_updi)`. Any segment whose UPDI address is in none of these windows shall cause `load_segments()` to return -1 with `"error: segment vaddr 0x%06x not in any programmable NVM window"` on `stderr`. The `--allow-lock-updi` CLI flag shall set `cfg.allow_lock_updi` and is forwarded to `updi_nvm_write_lockbits()` unchanged.

`parse_args()` shall recognise the option `--force-device=<family>` (case-insensitive value) and store the value in `cfg.force_device` (default `NULL`). The `--help` / `usage()` output shall list the option along with the five supported family names (`AVR-DA`, `AVR-DB`, `AVR-DD`, `AVR-DU`, `AVR-SD`). In normal startup (`app_main()`), after `updi_open()` succeeds, the application shall call `updi_select_device(cfg.updi_fd, cfg.force_device)` and shall treat a non-zero return as a fatal initialisation failure, exiting via the LLR-MAIN-07 teardown with exit code 1. In diagnostic mode (`run_device_mode()`, `--device`), `updi_select_device()` shall be called only when `cfg.force_device` is non-NULL and non-empty, so that unknown silicon can still be probed and its raw SIGROW bytes reported.

`app_main()` shall select the per-family device map between `elf_open()` and the first NVM access by calling `updi_select_device(cfg.updi_fd, cfg.force_device)` exactly once, where `cfg.force_device` is either the user-supplied `--force-device=<family>` string or `NULL`. When `cfg.force_device` is `NULL`, `updi_select_device()` shall determine the active family by SIGROW autodetect (LLR-UPDI-27). The ELF `.note.gnu.avr.deviceinfo` part-name shall NOT be used as a selection input; using it would defeat the mismatch check below by comparing the ELF family against the family the application just told the UPDI layer to be. After `updi_select_device()` returns 0, when `elf_ctx.device_name` is a recognised Microchip part-name (`updi_family_from_partname()` returns non-NULL) AND the user did NOT supply `--force-device`, the application shall verify that `updi_get_device()->family` matches the ELF-derived family string; on mismatch the application shall print `"error: ELF was built for <partname> (family <X>) but target reports <Y> (use --force-device=<Y> to override)"` to `stderr`, exit via the LLR-MAIN-07 teardown with code 1, and shall not call `updi_enter_debug()`, `load_segments()`, or `rsp_listen()`. The `--force-device=<family>` option is the documented escape hatch when the user knowingly wants to debug an ELF against a different silicon family (e.g. a generic AVR-DA build run on AVR-DB hardware) or when SIGROW autodetect cannot identify the part (AVR-DU/AVR-SD relocate SIGROW to a different base).

`parse_args()` shall recognise three new long-form flags and store them as bool fields on `AppConfig`: `--prog` sets `cfg.prog_mode = true`, `--no-verify` sets `cfg.no_verify = true`, and `--no-autobaud` sets `cfg.no_autobaud = true`. The usage banner shall document all three. The flag combination shall be validated: `--prog` is mutually exclusive with both `--device` and `--load` (specifying any pair shall print a usage error to `stderr` and call `exit(1)`); `--no-verify` is a no-op when `--device` is also given (no NVM writes happen in device mode); `--no-autobaud` is meaningful only in `--device` mode. Defaults are `false` for all three flags, preserving pre-Phase-9 behaviour for callers that supply none of them.

trace.name: Auto-Baud Link-Quality Probe in Device Mode

llr.text: `verify_segments(cfg, elf_ctx)` shall mirror the segment classification logic of `load_segments()` (FLASH / EEPROM / USERROW / FUSES / LOCK / SIGROW) but shall use `updi_nvm_read()` to read each programmed range back from the target in `CHUNK = 256`-byte windows and compare it against the ELF payload. Segments classified as SIGROW (read-only) and LOCK (read-once / lockbits become read-only post-write) shall be skipped. On a window mismatch the function shall compute `updi_crc32()` over the expected and actual buffers and print one `stderr` line per failing page reporting the window name, page-aligned VMA, and both CRC32 values. The function shall call `progress_render()` once per page and `progress_finish()` once per segment to drive the progress indicator. It shall return 0 when every byte of every verifiable segment matches and -1 otherwise. The caller is responsible for translating -1 into the process exit code `UPDI_EXIT_VERIFY_FAIL` (`2`).

`run_prog_mode(cfg)` shall implement the `--prog` operating mode. It shall: (1) open the ELF binary via `elf_open()`; (2) open the UPDI link via `updi_open(cfg->serial_device, cfg->baud_rate)` and call `updi_select_device(cfg->updi_fd, cfg->force_device)`; (3) print one `baud=<N>` line to `stdout` reporting the negotiated UART rate; (4) when `cfg->erase` is true, call `updi_chip_erase(cfg->updi_fd)`; (5) call `load_segments(cfg, &elf_ctx)` to program FLASH/EEPROM/USERROW/FUSES/LOCK; (6) unless `cfg->no_verify` is set, call `verify_segments(cfg, &elf_ctx)`; (7) on verify success print `verify: OK` to `stdout`; (8) close UPDI and ELF resources and return. The function shall NOT call `updi_enter_debug()` and shall NOT call `rsp_listen()` — the target is left running. Return-value mapping: 0 on success, 1 on any I/O / NVM failure, and `UPDI_EXIT_VERIFY_FAIL` (`2`) when verify reports a mismatch. The main dispatcher shall route to this function immediately after the device-info short-circuit when `cfg->prog_mode` is true.

The progress indicator shall be implemented by two static helpers `progress_render(phase, window, page, total_pages, percent)` and `progress_finish(void)`. When `isatty(STDOUT_FILENO)` is true `progress_render()` shall emit an in-place ANSI-friendly single-line bar of the form `[####....] PPP%% page N/M PHASE WINDOW` followed by carriage return (no newline) and `progress_finish()` shall emit a final newline to terminate the line. When `stdout` is not a TTY `progress_render()` shall emit one full newline-terminated line per call and `progress_finish()` shall be a no-op. Both helpers are called from `load_segments()`, `verify_segments()`, and `run_prog_mode()`. Additionally, `run_device_mode()` shall, after the existing SIGROW / REVID / ASI status print and unless `cfg->no_autobaud` is true, call `updi_probe_baud(cfg->serial_device, 8, autobaud_report_cb, NULL)` BEFORE opening the UPDI link and pass the selected rate to `updi_open()`; and shall, after the existing report, read the full FUSES window and the 4-byte LOCK window via `updi_nvm_read()` and emit the decode via `updi_format_fuses()` into a 2 KiB stack buffer.

trace.name: Auto-Baud Link-Quality Probe in Device Mode

llr.text: `parse_args()` shall recognise `--allow-erase` as a boolean flag (no argument) and set `cfg->allow_erase = true` when present. The default initialiser shall set the flag to `false`. The `usage()` help text shall include a one-paragraph description naming the verbs it unlocks (`monitor erase`, `monitor chip-erase`) so operators see the gating relationship without consulting the man page. The flag value shall be propagated to the constructed `RspContext` at server start by assigning `ctx.allow_erase = cfg->allow_erase ? 1 : 0;`, and the default breakpoint mode shall be set to `RSP_BP_MODE_SW` in the same initialiser block.

`parse_args()` shall recognise `--log` as a boolean flag (no argument) and set `cfg->log = true` when present. The default initialiser shall set the flag to `false`. The main orchestrator shall pass this flag to `rsp_set_logging()` (RSP front-end) and as the `log` argument to `dap_serve()` (DAP front-end), and `run_prog_mode()` shall emit per-phase programming diagnostics to `stderr` when it is set.

`parse_args()` shall recognise two mutually-exclusive boolean flags selecting the client protocol front-end: `--rsp` sets `cfg->dap_mode = false` and `--dap` sets `cfg->dap_mode = true`. The default initialiser shall set `cfg->dap_mode = false` (RSP). When both flags are supplied, `parse_args()` shall print `"--rsp and --dap are mutually exclusive"` to `stderr`, print the usage text, and `exit(1)`. After bring-up, `app_main()` shall dispatch on `cfg->dap_mode`: when true it shall call `dap_serve()` (the DAP front-end, `src/dap.c`) on the bound listener and debug-core handles; otherwise it shall run the existing RSP `event_loop()`. Both front-ends serve over the same `cfg.listen_fd` and UPDI link.

`parse_args()` shall recognise `--sleep` as a boolean flag that sets `cfg->debug_in_sleep = false`; the default initialiser shall set `cfg->debug_in_sleep = true` (debug-in-sleep enabled). Before the startup `updi_enter_debug()` call, `app_main()` shall apply the policy with `updi_set_debug_in_sleep(cfg.debug_in_sleep)` so the choice takes effect at that entry and every later re-entry (HLR-077, LLR-UPDI-35). The usage/`--help` text and the man page shall document that `--sleep` restores native target sleep (the debugger otherwise keeps the system clock alive so breakpoints fire after the firmware sleeps).

trace.name: Debug-in-Sleep (keep the system clock alive across SLEEP)

llr.text: `MAIN_NAME()` shall, before `parse_args()` and any device/ELF handling, scan `argv` for `--emit-vscode-config`; when present it shall call `emit_vscode_config()` — which writes a VS Code `launch.json` with a self-starting `request: "launch"` config (`avrosdb` type + `program`/`serial`/`elf`/`port`) and a `request: "attach"` alternative to stdout — and return 0 without touching the target. The usage/`--help` text shall document the flag.

`parse_args()` shall recognise `--start` and `--stop` as boolean flags setting `cfg->start_cpu` / `cfg->stop_cpu` (defaulting false), alongside the existing `--reset` (`cfg->reset_cpu`). When more than one of `--reset` / `--start` / `--stop` is given it shall print a diagnostic ("--reset, --start and --stop are mutually exclusive") and `exit(1)`. Each of the three modes shall make the `<elf-file>` operand optional (only `<serial-device>` is required); the missing-operand check shall therefore permit a single positional argument when any of `device_info`, `reset_cpu`, `start_cpu`, or `stop_cpu` is set.

`run_start_mode()` and `run_stop_mode()` shall each `updi_open()` the serial device (returning 1 with a wiring diagnostic on failure), then `updi_enter_debug()` to take OCD control; `run_start_mode()` shall then `updi_run()` the CPU and `run_stop_mode()` shall `updi_halt()` it. Both shall tear the link down with `updi_detach()` (LLR-UPDI-37) — leaving the target running / halted respectively rather than reset-and-released — print a one-line `start: OK (CPU running)` / `stop: OK (CPU halted)` confirmation to stdout, and return 0 (or 1 if the enter-debug/run/halt sequence failed). `MAIN_NAME()` shall dispatch to these after the `--device`, `--prog`, and `--reset` short-circuits and before installing signal handlers.

`main()` and `event_loop()` shall emit lifecycle log lines to `stderr` per HLR-065. Specifically: (a) immediately after `rsp_listen()` returns a non-negative fd in `app_main()`, print `"avrOSdb: listening on :%u
"` with `cfg.gdb_port`; (b) inside `event_loop()`, after every successful `rsp_accept()` that yields a non-negative fd, call `getpeername()` on the new fd and print `"avrOSdb: client connected from %s:%u
"` with the dotted-quad IPv4 address and port from the returned `sockaddr_in`; on `getpeername()` failure print `"avrOSdb: client connected from <unknown>
"`; (c) when `rsp_recv_packet()` returns 0 print `"avrOSdb: client disconnected (EOF)
"` before closing the fd, when it returns negative print `"avrOSdb: client disconnected (read error: %s)
"` with `strerror(errno)`; (d) after `rsp_dispatch_n()` returns, if `gdb_fd < 0` (the handler closed the socket) and `rctx.disconnect_reason != NULL`, print `"avrOSdb: client disconnected (%s)
"` with that reason and clear the field by setting it to `NULL`; if instead `gdb_fd >= 0` but `disconnect_reason != NULL` (vKill while listener-survival is still TODO), print the same line, then close `gdb_fd` and clear it locally; (e) immediately after `event_loop()` returns in `app_main()`, before the `teardown:` label runs, print `"avrOSdb: shutting down (%s)
"` where the reason is selected from a `volatile sig_atomic_t g_shutdown_signal` set by `sig_handler()` (`SIGINT`/`SIGTERM`) when applicable, defaulting to `"fatal: <best-effort context>"` for any other quit path. The signal handler shall record `signo` into `g_shutdown_signal` in addition to setting `g_quit = 1`. All log lines shall use `fprintf(stderr, ...)` followed by `fflush(stderr)`; no new flag gates them and they shall not be emitted on `stdout`. Duplicate emissions for the same transition are forbidden — only one disconnect line per fd-close.

function.title: src/updi.c — UPDI Physical Layer
function.name: updi
function.intro: Requirements for all public functions in `src/updi.c`: link initialisation, memory access, execution control, NVM programming, and console bridging.

llr.text: `updi_open()` shall open the UART device and configure it for 8E2 framing (8 data bits, even parity, 2 stop bits) in raw half-duplex mode using `termios`. `cfmakeraw()`, `CS8`, `CSTOPB`, `PARENB` (with `PARODD` cleared), and explicit baud setting via `cfsetispeed()`/`cfsetospeed()` shall be applied. If `tcsetattr()` returns `EINVAL` when setting `PARENB` (Linux PTY slaves strip parity from virtual terminals), the function shall retry with `PARENB` cleared so the link still works against PTY-backed test harnesses. The function shall return the open file descriptor on success or -1 on failure.

`updi_open()` shall execute up to three cold-start attempts. Attempt 0 (fast path) shall write a single 0x00 wake byte at the configured session baud rate, followed by `tcdrain()` and `tcflush(fd, TCIFLUSH)` to discard the half-duplex echo. Attempts 1 and 2 (slow path) shall instead generate a multi-millisecond line-low pulse by temporarily switching the kernel baud rate to 300 baud with `CSTOPB` cleared (1 stop bit) via `tcsetattr(TCSADRAIN)`, then writing two 0x00 bytes each followed immediately by `tcdrain()` to guarantee the byte is actually clocked out of the UART FIFO before the next operation. Each byte at 300 baud holds the TX line low for ≈33 ms (≥60 ms total — sufficient to reset the target's UPDI clock and contention detector on a cold power-on with passive single-wire combiners), and the half-duplex echoes are read-and-discarded at 300 baud. After both BREAK bytes, `updi_open()` shall sleep ≈50 ms (`nanosleep()`) so that any echo bytes still in flight on the line bus reach the kernel RX queue at 300-baud framing, then `tcflush(TCIFLUSH)` discards them. Only then shall the session baud rate be restored (`tcsetattr(TCSADRAIN)` followed by a second `tcflush(TCIFLUSH)`). Without `tcdrain()` after each write, the subsequent baud switch flushes or re-clocks the queued BREAK byte, destroying the line-low pulse; without the 50 ms settle, late echo bytes arrive AFTER the baud restore, get framed at 115200 baud, and desynchronise every subsequent frame echo. This mirrors avrdude's `serialupdi` programmer exactly (verified by `strace`) and is necessary because no portable POSIX API generates a multi-ms BREAK on demand — `tcsendbreak()` is too short and not honoured by all kernel UART drivers (notably the RPi PL011).

After the wake byte (attempt 0) or 300-baud double-break (attempts 1–2), `updi_open()` shall transmit `STCS ASI_CTRLB = ASI_CTRLB_CCDETDIS` (0x08) to disable the target's collision/contention detector, then `STCS ASI_CTRLA = ASI_CTRLA_IBDLY` (0x80) to enable inter-byte delay on the target's responses, then probe the link with `LDCS ASI_STATUSA` (opcode `0x80 | 0x00 = 0x80`). `ASI_STATUSA` carries UPDIREV in its upper nibble and is always readable while UPDI is enabled, including before any reset. If any STCS write or the LDCS probe fails, `updi_open()` shall advance to the next attempt. After 3 consecutive failed attempts the function shall return -1 and the caller shall treat the link as unavailable.

`updi_mem_read()` and `updi_mem_write()` shall transfer up to `UPDI_MAX_BLOCK` (256) bytes per UPDI burst using a three-frame sequence per datasheet §35.3.3.4: (1) a pointer-set frame — `ST_PTR_WORD` (`0x69`) followed by the 16-bit target address in little-endian order when `addr ≤ 0xFFFF`, or `ST_PTR_LONG` (`0x6A`) followed by the 24-bit address in little-endian order when `addr > 0xFFFF` — with a single ACK readback; (2) `REPEAT` (`0xA0`) followed by `(block_len - 1)`; (3) `LD ptr++` (`0x24`) for reads or `ST ptr++` (`0x64`) for writes. The pointer-set frame shall always use the 24-bit `ST_PTR_LONG` (`0x6A`) form regardless of the requested address (see LLR-UPDI-33, which mandates the 24-bit form unconditionally to avoid the stale-high-byte hazard); the 16-bit `ST_PTR_WORD` (`0x69`) form is never used. The 24-bit form covers every address, including the AVR128DA/DB mapped-Flash region above 64 KiB. If `len` exceeds `UPDI_MAX_BLOCK`, the function shall split the request into consecutive bursts automatically, with no size restriction imposed on the caller.

`updi_mem_read()` shall use `select()` with a 100 ms timeout before each `read()` call on the UART file descriptor to enforce a per-byte inactivity deadline. If `select()` returns zero (timeout) before a byte is available, the function shall abandon the current transaction and return -1.
`updi_mem_write()` shall write arbitrary byte ranges to the SRAM address space of the target using UPDI ST commands and return 0 on success or -1 on UART framing error, timeout, or UPDI NAK.

`updi_nvm_write_flash()` shall require `word_addr` to be aligned to a 512-byte FLASH page boundary and `len` to be a non-zero multiple of 512. It shall enter NVM programming mode by transmitting the `KEY` opcode (`0xE0`) with the 8-byte string `"NVMProg "`, asserting reset with `STCS ASI_RESET_REQ = 0x59`, releasing reset with `STCS ASI_RESET_REQ = 0x00`, then polling `ASI_SYS_STATUS` via LDCS for bit 3 (NVMPROG, mask `0x08`) up to 100 iterations (≈ 100 ms). For each page it shall write the page data via `updi_mem_write()`, write `0x03` (ERWP) to `NVMCTRL_CTRLA`, and poll `NVMCTRL_STATUS` bit 0 (BUSY) clear up to 20 iterations (≈ 20 ms). On exit it shall toggle `ASI_RESET_REQ` `0x59` then `0x00` to release the target. Timeout of either poll shall return -1; a `NVMCTRL_STATUS` WRERR (bit 2) shall return `UPDI_ERR_WP`.

`updi_halt()` shall halt the CPU by writing `ASI_OCD_CTRLA_STOP` (0x01) to `ASI_OCD_CTRLA` via STCS, then polling `ASI_OCD_STATUS` via LDCS for bit `ASI_OCD_STATUS_STOPPED` (0x01) set. The function shall return 0 once the STOPPED bit is observed and -1 on UPDI failure or if the bit does not become set within the LDCS poll budget.

`updi_step()` shall single-step the halted CPU by setting `OCD_CTRL0_STEP` (0x04) in `OCD_CTRL0` (UPDI byte address `0x0F88`) via STS, then writing `ASI_OCD_CTRLA_RUN` (0x02) to `ASI_OCD_CTRLA` via STCS to release the CPU for exactly one instruction, then polling `ASI_OCD_STATUS.STOPPED` until set. Returns 0 on success, -1 on UPDI failure.

`updi_run()` shall resume the halted CPU by writing `ASI_OCD_CTRLA_RUN` (0x02) to `ASI_OCD_CTRLA` via STCS and shall return 0 immediately without polling — callers that need to wait for a subsequent halt shall use `updi_ocd_poll_halted()` directly. Returns -1 on UPDI failure.

`updi_mem_read()` shall be callable while the target CPU is in the RUNNING state (not halted). The function shall not call `updi_halt()` internally, permitting non-intrusive SRAM sampling for the monitor sub-commands and console polling without interrupting firmware execution.

`updi_console_poll()` shall perform a background `updi_mem_read()` of the avrOS software UART output buffer and return any pending bytes to the caller without halting the CPU. The function shall return the number of bytes read (0 if none pending) or -1 on UPDI error.

`updi_read_device_info(fd, info)` shall populate the caller-supplied `UpdiDeviceInfo` struct with: 3 SIGROW DEVICEID bytes from physical address `0x1100`-`0x1102` (datasheet §7.6.1, Table 7-4), the SYSCFG.REVID byte at `0x0F01` (datasheet §8.3.2.1; SYSCFG base `0x0F00`), 16 SERNUM bytes at `0x1110`-`0x111F` (datasheet §7.6.2.3), and the three ASI registers `ASI_SYS_STATUS`, `ASI_KEY_STATUS`, `ASI_STATUSB` read via `LDCS`. The function shall be non-destructive (no halt, no NVM activity). On any UPDI read failure it shall set `info->fail_op` to a short ASCII tag (`"sigrow"`, `"revid"`, `"sernum"`, `"sys-status"`, `"key-status"`, `"asi-statusb"`) and return -1; on success it shall set `info->fail_op = NULL` and return 0.
